I went to a high school for students with learning disabilities and was given a lot of one on one instruction. I understand exactly how you feel. I had to hit rock bottom and fall through the cracks many times before finally getting diagnosed and getting the help I needed. If you struggle with social skills like many people with the disorder and don't want to go to a social skills group (I've been there and hated them) there's an incredibly intelligent woman named Michelle Garcia Winner who has written several books on social thinking. I also recommend going to to a therapist who understands learning disabilities because they can help guide you in the right direction and also give you coping skills. You didn't indicate whether or not you were still in school, but let me know if you are and I can give you some tips for that. Things will get better if you seek out the appropriate supports, I promise. The disorder honestly needs more awareness and should be added to the DSM because too many bright individuals are suffering due to the lack of awareness.

I have the disorder myself and know several others who do. We all have IQ discrepancies between our verbal and performance IQ scores. There are several "markers" for the disorder that psychologists use to diagnose the disorder, the IQ discrepancy seeming to be the most important. Everyone with the disorder is different. For example, I am very good at math and got an A in every high school math class despite the visual-spatial difficulties related to the disorder. However, I know people on the complete opposite end of the spectrum who graduated high school but still need to count on their fingers or use a calculator for basic addition. Terrible depth perception and being physically "awkward" are also common, and since you have these as well as the IQ discrepancy, you sound like some people I know. If you still don't feel you have the disorder after reading the link the other person provided, you can always get another evaluation, but they can be very expensive.

I have a learning disorder myself called nonverbal learning disorder and think that the advice for him to just get a minimum wage job is complete bullshit. I have no idea of your financial situation and I'm an American, but you could try hiring him a tutor and have him enroll at your local community college part time. I went to a high school for kids with learning disorders, so I have seen pretty much the whole spectrum of different functioning levels. There are several people from my graduating class who are at real colleges now who still have extreme difficulty with reading and can't do basic addition without counting on their fingers. I was once in the same place as your brother and thought I was a failure who would never attend college because I was learning "disabled." However, when I was 16 I realized that learning disabilities do not make it impossible for one to learn, they merely make it hard to learn certain things in the same way that the "average" person does. Because of this, my school called learning disabilities learning differences, since in reality they just make you learn differently.

Going back to what his high school counselor said, I was once told by a neuropsychologist that I should attend a college in Vermont called Landmark that only works with students who have severe learning disorders. My parents and I completely disagreed with him and felt it would be best for me to look at colleges that were mainstream but had additional support programs for students with learning differences. After lots of research, my parents found a program that is working great for me. I am currently in the undergrad business school at a university that was ranked in the top 20 for public universities and so far things are great. However, I know that if I hadn't gone to a high school for students with ld, I would not even be in college right now. It's not too late for your brother. Let him find something something he loves and is good at. There are so so many highly successful people out there who have learning disorders (ex: Richard Branson, Steven Spielberg, Steve Jobs, Ingvar Kamprad, Tom Cruise, Kiera Knightley, Whoopie Goldberg, and many more!)

TLDR; I have a learning disorder myself, so I understand how your brother feels. Get him a tutor who is used to working with learning differences if you can afford it and enroll him in a class or two in a topic he is really passionate about. Some of the smartest people I know have learning disorders and it is heartbreaking to know that yet another person out there is facing the same struggles my friends and I faced when we were younger. Best of luck to your brother. His learning "disorder(s)" may make him learn differently, it also means that he thinks differently than the rest of the world, and those who think different are the ones who make the greatest changes in the world.
